body: Shoes on. Now, please. Twenty past eight on a school morning, and a woman at the bottom of the stairs is saying her son’s name for the third time. From the landing there is a shifting sound and then a voice, entirely calm, saying that he heard her the first time. He is telling the truth. He heard her the first time and the second and this one, and he is still sitting on the edge of his bed with one shoe in his hand and the other somewhere under it. She stands there with the car keys and cannot think of a thing to say back, because as a defence it is unanswerable. He did hear.

In English he has used the word correctly, and that is the whole trouble. There is a word for what she actually wanted from him and it is a different word, and the gap between the two is where the entire argument was living.

Hear, O Israel. In English that is a request for attention, and it is complete the moment attention has been given. A person can hear a thing, understand it fully, decline it, and have used the word properly from beginning to end.

Shema does not divide that way. The same word covers the hearing, the understanding and the doing, and it is used across all three without a seam — not as a metaphor, and not as a pious stretching of the meaning, but as ordinary usage. It is the word for listening and it is also the word for obeying, and the language does not offer a convenient way to have the first without the second. A child who has been told and has not done it has not, in that construction, heard. Obedience is not a second step that follows listening once listening has finished. It is part of what the listening was.

Every English translation has to pick one side of that and lose the other. Hear loses the doing. Obey loses the listening. There is no English word that holds both at once, which is why the Hebrew word so often survives untranslated in the mouths of people who use English for everything else.

Take that seriously and a good deal of comfortable ground disappears. In English you can hear a thing perfectly and do nothing about it, and no one has misused the word. In Hebrew that is not available. There is no category for the man who has understood the teaching, agreed with it warmly, discussed it at some length and not moved — he is not a slow starter and he is not a work in progress, he is somebody who has not heard. That is a harder standard than most of us would set for ourselves. It is also the standard the text is using while we read it.

Our information culture is built on exactly the gap the English word leaves open. It is possible now to be enormously well taught and entirely unpractised — to have listened to a great deal of good teaching, understood it, agreed with it, recommended it to somebody else, and be standing precisely where you were standing before. That is not hypocrisy. Hypocrisy knows what it is doing. This is subtler and far more common: a genuine, warm, attentive hearing that terminates in itself, and that feels like obedience while it is going on, because from the inside agreement and action are so nearly indistinguishable.

That single feature changes a great deal of the text once you can see it. Every command to hear becomes a command to comply. Every complaint that the people would not hear stops being about attention and becomes about refusal. And the daily confession that opens with the word stops being an appeal for quiet before something important is said. It becomes a statement about how the rest of the day is going to be conducted.
It also explains a tone in the prophets that reads oddly in English. They do not sound like men complaining about attention spans. They sound like men who have been ignored.

Which is not an argument against study, and it would be a poor one. Understanding matters. People do wrong things sincerely all the time for want of it, and a faith that never asks what a text means will end up meaning whatever its holder needed it to mean. But study has a failure mode of its own, and it is not error. It is completion. A subject can be closed. A person can finish a book on generosity and come away with the settled feeling of a matter dealt with — and the feeling is entirely honest, and nothing in the bank account changes. The hearing was real. It simply ended where the reading did.
In this language, a thing heard and not done was not heard.

There is a man who has driven the same forty minutes to a distribution centre for nine years, and for most of them the drive was talk radio and an argument he was having in his head with somebody who was not in the car. A cousin put a station on for him in April, more or less to stop him talking, and he left it because changing it would have meant a decision at a roundabout. What he noticed a few weeks later was not that he felt more spiritual. It was that he had started saying good morning to the security man on the gate, whose name he had not previously known and now knows. He would not connect those two facts if you put them to him.

Nothing was taught to him at that gate. Something got into the forty minutes before it, repeatedly, for weeks, and then a hand went up at a barrier. That is the whole distance between hearing and doing, and it is shorter than it is usually made to look.

The honest difficulty with all this is that it can be turned into a whip inside a fortnight. A word that fuses hearing and doing is very easily used to inspect other people, and more easily still turned on yourself at two in the morning, when everything you have heard and not done is available in a single list and none of it can be acted on before daylight. Nothing in the text asks for that. It is simply what an anxious mind does with a good idea.

But the answer to that is not to go back to the softer word. It is to notice what the fused word actually implies, which is a lightening rather than a load. If hearing and doing are one motion, then the doing is not a separate performance you have to summon afterwards out of your own resources. It is what hearing turns into when nothing interrupts it. Most of the failure is not a collapse of will at the end. It is an interruption very near the beginning.

So the word is not linguistic trivia and it is not a rebuke. It is a description of a shape. What goes in comes out unless something stops it, and the ordinary thing that stops it is that the hearing was arranged as an event — a session, a sermon, a book — with a beginning and a satisfying end. Hearing that has been designed to finish will duly finish. That is all it was ever built to do.
All of which is theory until something is actually playing in the car. So here is the part that is not theory.

The dial runs from HM 300.30 to HM 398.70 and carries 121 stations, arranged the way a broadcast band is arranged rather than the way a library is. Ministry stations sit together, the nations sit together in their own languages, the always-on formats sit together, and once you know roughly where a block is you stop needing to look for it. 46 frequencies are on air at this moment, and every one is playing without waiting to be asked what you are in the mood for. There is no queue to assemble and nothing to name before it will start.

Start at HM 313.80 — The Ancient Paths. It is the Middle Eastern frequency, and it belongs at the end of this particular argument because it is the station that sounds like the place the word came from. The modes are not the ones a Western ear settles into. The ornament is different, the scales land slightly off from where you expect them to, and the effect is that for the first fortnight you cannot quite reduce it to wallpaper. It will not let you. Which is an odd thing to recommend a station for, except that the whole subject here is hearing that refuses to complete itself in the ear. Put it on for the drive, and let it be a little foreign for a while.

There is nothing to install. No app, no download and no card. Open kJubilee.com on whatever phone is nearest, press play, and it plays — it is built deliberately for inexpensive phones and thin connections, so it starts on the hardware people actually have. If you want it closer to hand, add the page to your home screen and it opens like anything else on it. And do make yourself an account while you are there. It is free, it keeps your favourites with you across every Jubilee site, and it is how the band finds out which frequencies people are actually reaching for — which is how the next one gets built.

So do not consider it, and do not look into it. Those are hearing words of exactly the kind this article has been about: they feel like a response and they commit to nothing whatever. Put HM 313.80 on this afternoon while you are doing something else, and leave it running through a fortnight of ordinary days. The word means hear, and then it means do, and the smallest available version of doing is a number, a press, and a room that is no longer quiet.
